title: Why did people listen for the beeps of Sputnik 1?
answer: In October 1957, the Soviet Union sent a small metal ball into orbit around Earth. It was called Sputnik 1 and was the first artificial satellite. Its thin antennas sent a repeating radio signal. People on the ground could use radio equipment to hear it as a stream of beeps. A device made on Earth was now going around our planet again and again, much as the Moon does.
facts: Sputnik 1 was about as wide as a large beach ball.

title: What surprising clue did Explorer 1 find above Earth?
answer: Explorer 1 was the first U.S. satellite, launched in January 1958. One instrument counted energetic particles. The counts sometimes dropped to zero in places where scientists had expected to find some particles. The researchers worked out that the instrument could be getting more hits than it could count, rather than no hits at all. Later measurements helped confirm a radiation belt around Earth, where our planet’s magnetic field holds many energetic particles.
facts: Explorer 1 was a long narrow spacecraft with instruments built into its body.

title: Who rode Vostok 1 around Earth?
aliases: Who was the first human in space
answer: In April 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first human to travel into space. He rode in a round cabin on a Soviet spacecraft called Vostok 1. It went around Earth once before coming back down. Only a few years earlier, Sputnik had gone into orbit with no one aboard. Gagarin’s journey showed that a person could travel all the way around our planet in space and return.
facts: A Russian space traveler is often called a cosmonaut.

title: How many times did John Glenn circle Earth in Friendship 7?
answer: In 1962, John Glenn rode a small spacecraft named Friendship 7 around Earth three times. He was the first American to go into orbit. Other American astronauts had already reached space, but their short trips came back before making a full circle. Glenn stayed in space for just under five hours. A thick shield helped protect his capsule from heat as it rushed back through Earth’s air.
facts: The capsule landed in the Atlantic Ocean.

title: Why did Ed White step outside Gemini 4?
answer: In 1965, astronaut Ed White opened a hatch and moved outside the Gemini 4 spacecraft. He wore a suit that supplied air and protected him from the space around him. A line kept him joined to the spacecraft while he floated beside it. White tested how it felt to move out there. Knowing how to work outside a spacecraft would help later crews build and fix things in orbit.
facts: White’s trip outside was the first spacewalk by an American astronaut.

title: What did the Apollo 8 crew see when they flew around the Moon?
answer: In December 1968, NASA sent three astronauts on a trip around the Moon. They were the first people to see the Moon up close from orbit. Their spacecraft passed over the far side, the side we usually cannot see from Earth. During the trip, the astronauts saw Earth come into view above the gray Moon. A photo taken by crew member Bill Anders became known as Earthrise.
facts: Apollo 8 circled the Moon ten times without landing.

title: How did Apollo 13 come home after trouble on the way to the Moon?
aliases: How did astronauts get home Apollo 13
answer: In April 1970, Apollo 13 was on its way to the Moon when an oxygen tank broke. It damaged part of the spacecraft, so the astronauts gave up the planned landing. They used the small lunar lander as a shelter while they traveled around the Moon and back toward Earth. The crew and teams on the ground worked together to save power and keep the spacecraft safe. All three astronauts returned alive.
facts: The lunar lander that served as a shelter was called Aquarius.

title: Why did Apollo 15 take a car to the Moon?
aliases: hammer and feather on Moon Apollo 15
answer: Apollo 15 landed on the Moon in 1971. The crew took a small electric vehicle called a lunar rover, so they could visit spots far beyond their landing place. They drove near mountains and a deep channel, took photographs, and collected rocks. The vehicle folded up for the trip to the Moon. Unfolding it gave the astronauts a way to carry tools and samples without taking every step on foot.
facts: Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather. Without much air on the Moon to slow the feather, both landed together.

title: What was it like to live and work in Skylab?
aliases: what did people study on Skylab
answer: Skylab was the first U.S. space station. Astronauts visited it in 1973 and 1974 to study the Sun, try experiments, and see what happens to people who live in orbit for weeks. Part of the station was hurt during launch, leaving it too warm. The first crew put up a shade and made other repairs. That made the station a place they could work and sleep in.
facts: The third Skylab crew lived in space for about 84 days.

title: Why did the space shuttle have wings?
aliases: how did NASA space shuttle work
answer: NASA’s space shuttle rose into the sky with rocket power and worked in orbit as a spacecraft. At the end of a trip, the winged part came back through the air and glided onto a runway. It did not use jet engines to land. NASA could prepare that part to fly again. The shuttle carried satellites and helped build the International Space Station by bringing up large pieces.
facts: The reusable winged part was called the orbiter.

title: How did people make the Mir space station bigger in orbit?
aliases: when was Russian Mir space station assembled
answer: Mir started with one section sent to orbit in 1986. Later flights brought other rooms and work areas to join to it. Putting the parts together in space meant the whole station did not need to fit inside one rocket. Crews could live on Mir while working on experiments. In the 1990s, U.S. space shuttles came to the station to bring people and supplies.
facts: Mir’s first section came from the Soviet Union.

title: What kinds of things can Chandra see with X-rays?
aliases: what does Chandra X ray telescope see
answer: The Chandra X-ray Observatory is a telescope in space. It looks for X-rays that some extremely hot places give off. These rays come from regions such as gas around a black hole or material heated by a star’s explosion. Earth’s air blocks most X-rays from space, so Chandra works above it. Observations like these can show parts of the sky that ordinary cameras would miss.
facts: A shuttle brought Chandra to space in 1999.

title: How did Spitzer see through some clouds of space dust?
aliases: how to see stars through space dust
answer: Spitzer was a NASA space telescope that collected infrared light, which human eyes cannot see. Some infrared light gets through dust that can hide stars from an ordinary telescope. That let Spitzer pick out young stars in dusty clouds. It also measured infrared light from distant planets and galaxies. Different kinds of light give scientists different clues, so they often compare pictures taken by several telescopes.
facts: Spitzer began its mission in 2003.

title: How did Kepler notice planets it could not photograph?
answer: NASA’s Kepler space telescope watched many stars and measured how bright they looked. If a planet crossed in front of a star as seen from the telescope, it could block a little light. A tiny dip that happened again and again gave scientists a clue that a planet might be there. The mission found many planets outside our solar system, including some smaller than Neptune.
facts: The original Kepler survey watched one main patch of sky for years.

title: Why does TESS search for planets around bright stars?
answer: The TESS telescope looks at a large part of the sky in sections. It measures the light of stars, looking for small dips when possible planets cross their faces. The mission helps find planets around nearby bright stars. A planet is usually easier for other telescopes to study when its star is bright enough to give them a stronger signal. Follow-up observations help scientists check which tiny dips really came from planets.
facts: TESS stands for Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite.

title: How did Gaia help build a three-dimensional map of the Milky Way?
aliases: how did Gaia map the Milky Way
answer: The European Space Agency’s Gaia spacecraft measured where stars appeared in the sky. It took measurements again and again as it moved along with Earth around the Sun. Some nearby stars appeared to shift very slightly against more distant ones when viewed from different places. That shift helped scientists find their distances. The measurements also helped show how stars move through our galaxy.
facts: Gaia’s maps cover more than a billion stars.

title: What kinds of cold places did Herschel study in space?
answer: The Herschel observatory studied long waves of infrared light from cold gas and dust, neither of which has to shine brightly to give off such light. It could look at clouds where new stars were beginning to form before they were easy to see in ordinary photographs. It could also find signs of molecules in space. Herschel’s large mirror helped gather weak light from distant places.
facts: Herschel was a European Space Agency observatory with a mirror about 3.5 meters wide.

title: What did Galileo learn by circling Jupiter?
answer: NASA’s Galileo spacecraft entered orbit around Jupiter in 1995. It could pass many times through the region around the planet and study several moons up close. Measurements near Europa pointed to a salty ocean hidden below the ice. A smaller part of the mission plunged into Jupiter’s clouds and sent back measurements as it went deeper. The main spacecraft kept flying around Jupiter after the probe stopped.
facts: Galileo was the first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter.

title: Why did Juno fly over Jupiter’s poles?
answer: Juno circles Jupiter on a path that passes over the north and south poles. This gave its cameras a view of places that are difficult to see from Earth. The spacecraft showed storms gathered around both poles. Other instruments studied the planet’s magnetic field and measured microwaves to study the atmosphere beneath the bright cloud tops. Jupiter has no solid ground for a rover to drive across.
facts: Many of Jupiter’s big storms are part of patterns scientists can track from orbit.

title: What could Cassini learn by going around Saturn for years?
aliases: what did Cassini discover about Saturn
how did Cassini find plumes on Enceladus
answer: The Cassini spacecraft began orbiting Saturn in 2004. Instead of seeing the planet and its rings on a single pass, it could watch as things changed and visit different moons. Cassini observed jets of material coming from the icy moon Enceladus. It also brought a smaller spacecraft named Huygens to land on Titan. At the end of its mission, Cassini flew into Saturn’s atmosphere.

title: What did Huygens find under Titan’s orange haze?
answer: Huygens was a small European spacecraft carried to Saturn by Cassini. In 2005 it drifted down to Titan by parachute as cameras and instruments studied the thick air. Below the haze, it saw hills cut by dark channels. The lander touched down on a surface scattered with rounded pieces that may be water ice. Huygens sent its measurements to Cassini for the trip back to Earth by radio.

title: What did New Horizons find when it flew past Pluto?
answer: In July 2015, NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft made the first close visit to Pluto. It found mountains and a broad bright region shaped like part of a heart. The bright plain there contains frozen nitrogen. New Horizons moved past Pluto instead of stopping in orbit. Years later, it passed Arrokoth, a smaller object in the Kuiper Belt that looks like two rounded pieces joined together.

answer: Pioneer 10 left Earth in 1972 and became the first spacecraft to pass through the main asteroid belt. It then flew by Jupiter and sent back close measurements of the great planet and its surroundings. Before that trip, scientists knew about Jupiter’s colors from pictures made much closer to home. Pioneer 10 could measure conditions near the planet itself, and helped NASA plan later trips far from Earth.

title: How did Mariner 2 learn that Venus is very hot?
answer: Mariner 2 flew past Venus in 1962. Thick clouds hide the planet’s ground in ordinary photographs, but the spacecraft could measure invisible waves coming from Venus. The readings supported the idea that the surface below those clouds is very hot. Mariner 2 did not land or circle the planet. Its instruments took measurements as the spacecraft passed, then it continued traveling around the Sun.
facts: Mariner 2 made the first successful scientific flyby of another planet.

title: How did Magellan map land it could not see through the clouds?
answer: NASA’s Magellan orbited Venus in the 1990s. Thick clouds hide the ground from cameras that see ordinary light. Magellan sent radio waves toward the surface instead. It listened for the waves that bounced back and used them to build up pictures of the ground. These radar pictures showed mountains, old impact holes, and shapes made by lava across much of the planet.
facts: Scientists can use radar to make an image without sunlight.

title: What did the Viking landers do on Mars?
answer: In 1976, two Viking missions brought U.S. spacecraft to the surface of Mars. Each mission included a spacecraft that stayed in orbit and another that landed. The landers took pictures, checked the weather, and studied soil. Some experiments looked for signs of life, but their results did not show clear proof that anything was alive there. Each lander remained at its landing spot and could send pictures back from the same place over time.

The rover could roll up to nearby rocks, look at them closely, and help scientists study what they were made of. answer: InSight landed on Mars and placed a sensitive instrument on the ground. A seismometer can notice tiny shakes that people might not feel. The shakes from marsquakes traveled through the planet at different speeds. Researchers used their arrival times to learn about layers deep under the surface, including the central core. answer: The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter looks down from above the planet. Its cameras can make maps sharp enough to show features that a small rover would take a long time to reach. Scientists compare pictures to find good routes and interesting rocks. answer: Phoenix stayed in one spot near the northern part of Mars. In 2008 it used a moving arm to dig into the soil, scooping up bits for its instruments. answer: NASA’s MAVEN spacecraft flew around Mars and studied the thin air high above the ground. It measured how particles escape into space. Light from the Sun and streams of particles from it can help knock parts of the outer air away. Those measurements gave scientists clues about how Mars lost much of its atmosphere over a very long time. The thinner air affects what happens to liquid water at the surface.

answer: Dawn traveled to Vesta and Ceres, two large worlds in the asteroid belt. Vesta is mostly rocky. Ceres has more water and shows a very different surface. Dawn carried instruments that could map the shapes and test what different parts of each world were made of. Visiting both helped scientists compare what happened to two objects that formed in the same broad neighborhood of the solar system.

title: Why did Rosetta travel beside a comet around the Sun?
answer: Rosetta was a European spacecraft that caught up with a comet named 67P. It stayed near the comet for many months. answer: The ICESat-2 satellite sends tiny flashes of laser light toward Earth. An instrument waits for some of that light to bounce back. title: Why did Voyager take a record of sounds from Earth?
